Proposition: The literature establishes three recurrent margins determining the welfare effect of AI regulation: externality materiality, decision-relevant information production, and fixed-cost incidence on entry and experimentation.
Confidence Status: Mechanisms established; joint policy ranking conditional
Major Falsifier: Comparable AI-governance treatments show these margins do not condition regulatory effects.

Proposition: Competitive incidence depends on the layer of the AI value chain at which governance attaches; rules can open a bottleneck, burden entrants or shift market power vertically.
Principal Boundary: Bottleneck location; learning technology; switching; complements
Major Falsifier: Layer/bottleneck location does not predict entry, switching, access or rent shifting under comparable interventions.

Proposition: Behaviourally effective accountability mechanisms require a chain connecting usable evidence to sufficiently independent evaluation, decision authority and credible consequences.
Major Falsifier: Reliable outcomes improve from disclosure/audit alone where signals are unusable, authority absent and consequences unchanged.

Proposition: The welfare ranking of international coordination versus differentiated/polycentric governance depends on cross-border externalities, verifiability and enforceable control points.
Principal Boundary: Externality location; verifiability; enforceable control point
Evidence Provenance: Institutional + cross-domain transfer; limited direct causal evidence
Major Falsifier: Direct comparative evidence shows robust welfare superiority of one coordination form across materially different externality and enforcement structures.
